extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and agents who practice or seek to practice before the United States Patent and Trademark Office; USPTO disciplinary counsel and regulated practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing authorized practice before the USPTO, practitioner duties (communication, fee division), prohibitions on assisting suspended/excluded practitioners, evidentiary and sanctioning rules, and appellate review procedures used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice before the Office' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Practice before the Office' includes, but is not limited to, any law-related service that comprehends any matter connected with the presentation to the Office or any of its officers or employees relating to a client's rights, privileges, duties, or responsibilities under the laws or regulations administered by the Office for the grant of a patent or registration of a trademark. This includes 'preparing necessary documents in contemplation of filing the documents with the Office ... as well as communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples treated as practice before the Office: drafting patent applications and responses to office actions; identifying oneself as attorney-of-record; counseling clients about options for prosecuting patents; strategizing about filings. Case examples cited: In re Piccone; discussion that continued advising/communicating about matters pending before the USPTO constitutes practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on practicing in a jurisdiction in violation / assisting another in doing so (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction, or assist another in doing so. The USPTO is considered a jurisdiction for purposes of this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove a violation, the Director must establish that the other person engaged in unauthorized practice before the Office and that the registered practitioner facilitated such practice. Remaining attorney-of-record or otherwise enabling a suspended/excluded practitioner's client communications or filings can constitute assistance. Cited precedent: In re Banger Shia and case law on USPTO jurisdiction (Sperry, Kroll v. Finnerty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on aiding a suspended or excluded practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(e) (2013) / § 11.58(h) (post-amendment))
rubrics_metrics.description: A provision in effect at the time (and amended later) prohibits a suspended or excluded practitioner from aiding another practitioner in the other practitioner's practice before the Office unless the disciplined practitioner is a salaried employee under the practitioner's direct supervision. Even then, the disciplined practitioner may not 'communicate directly in writing, orally, or otherwise with a client of the other practitioner in regard to any immediate or prospective business before the Office' nor 'render any legal advice or any legal services to a client of the other practitioner in regard to any immediate or prospective business before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible intermediary arrangements (e.g., foreign agents or corporate liaisons) are distinct and conditioned on client consent after full disclosure and the intermediary's status; they do not authorize arrangements with suspended/excluded individuals. Failure to comply (e.g., allowing suspended practitioner to remain point of contact, continue counseling, receive fees) supports finding of assisting unauthorized practice. Cited decisions: In re Colitz, Piccone, Kroll.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to withdraw or change correspondence address after suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(b)(1)(i)(c) context)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who has been suspended or excluded must not remain as the attorney-of-record or fail to withdraw or change the correspondence address for applications; failing to do so can result in correspondence being sent to a suspended practitioner and constitute unauthorized practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in record: Office actions mailed to suspended practitioner because no notice of withdrawal/change of correspondence address was filed. Such failure is evidence of continued practice before the Office and supports disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of legal fees between practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b) and (e))
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing fees between practitioners who are not in the same firm, a division may be made only if: (1) the division is in proportion to the services performed by each practitioner or each practitioner assumes joint responsibility for the representation; (2) the client agrees to the arrangement, including the share each practitioner will receive, and the agreement is confirmed in writing; and (3) the total fee is reasonable. Section 11.105(b) requires communication of the basis or rate of the fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose fee division and obtain clients' written consent violates the rule. The ABA formal opinion relied upon by a respondent is not binding on USPTO; even the ABA opinion recommends appropriate disclosures. Evidence that a non-registered/suspended practitioner set fees or unilaterally collected and allocated fees is relevant to violation. The total fee's reasonableness also remains a requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner's duties to communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.102(a), 11.104(a)(2), 11.104(a)(3), 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must abide by a client's decisions concerning the objectives of the representation and consult with the client as to the means by which objectives are to be pursued (11.102(a)). Practitioners must reasonably consult with clients regarding means to accomplish objectives (11.104(a)(2)), keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter and explain matters reasonably necessary to permit informed decisions (11.104(a)(3) and (b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of rarely communicating with clients, failing to provide contact information, or having clients unaware of who is handling their matters supports violations. Specific harms (e.g., clients not informed of abandonment of applications) are factual consequences considered in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.804(c) proscribes 'conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing a suspended practitioner to continue counseling clients, using a registered practitioner's name and customer number for filings while the other practitioner was suspended, or otherwise deceiving clients regarding who is representing them can constitute violations under this provision. The order cites In re Lane and other precedent in defining deceit and misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.804(d) proscribes conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice — behavior that negatively impacts the public's perception of the legal system or undermines confidence in the legal profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized practice of law is regarded as a serious threat to the effective administration of justice; allowing suspended practitioners to operate undermines public confidence. Case citations and authorities support this as a basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. 'Evidence is clear 'if it is certain, unambiguous, and plain to the understanding,' and it is convincing 'if it is reasonable and persuasive enough to cause the trier of facts to believe it.'' (quotation from Foster v. AlliedSignal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director must meet the clear-and-convincing standard; the decision explains how facts showing ongoing advising/communication, failure to withdraw, fee arrangements, and lack of client knowledge satisfy that standard in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standards in USPTO disciplinary hearings (37 C.F.R. § 11.50 and precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of evidence prevailing in courts of law and equity are not controlling in hearings in disciplinary proceedings; hearsay is admissible in USPTO disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents' objections based on hearsay are routinely rejected; case law (e.g., Colitz, Kroll) supports admission of hearsay. The Director and ALJ may rely on such evidence in establishing violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal review authority and standard (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55, 11.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director reviews an appeal from an ALJ initial decision on the record before the ALJ and has authority to conduct a de novo review of the factual record. The Director may affirm, reverse, or modify the initial decision or remand the matter for further proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appellant may raise legal and factual arguments on appeal; the Director's de novo authority permits independent review of both facts and law. Citations include Jyfarinangeli v. Lehman and the cited regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning framework and factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing discipline, the relevant factors include: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALJs and the Director weigh these factors in determining appropriate sanction (suspension, exclusion, length). The order discusses application: duties violated (communication, authorization), knowledge/intent, actual harm (abandoned applications), aggravators (dishonest motive, substantial experience) and mitigator (absence of prior record). Precedent cases (Piccone, Achterhof, Kroll) inform sanctioning expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on use of corporate liaisons and foreign agents as intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance allows a registered practitioner to rely upon the advice of a corporate liaison or a client/patent applicant's foreign agent as to actions to be taken before the Office so long as the practitioner is aware that the client has consented after full disclosure to be represented by the liaison or agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This intermediary framework is narrowly applied: it does not permit arrangements with suspended/excluded individuals or individuals who are not corporate liaisons/foreign agents. Client consent after full disclosure is required; absence of such consent precludes treating an intermediary as proper. Cited Office Gazettes (1086 OG 457; 1091 OG 26) and In re Colitz.

rubrics_metrics.name: State bar/licensure status and constitutional claims are not defenses to USPTO discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's active state law license or First Amendment claims do not excuse violations of USPTO regulations; the USPTO has exclusive authority to admit and discipline practitioners before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Sperry v. Florida, Kroll v. Finnerty, Correll decisions; regulation of professions is permissible when rationally related to fitness to practice; practitioners waive or are subject to rules by registering to practice before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice of discipline (37 C.F.R. § 11.59)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where discipline is imposed, the Director shall give notice of the public discipline and the reasons for the discipline to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the states where the respondent is admitted, to courts where the respondent is known to be admitted, and to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final orders will be distributed pursuant to the regulation; this is part of the remedy and administrative process following a sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative precedent and factual indicators of unauthorized practice and assisting it
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant factual indicators include: a suspended practitioner continuing to advise clients about USPTO matters; remaining attorney-of-record while suspended; being the primary point of client contact; unapproved fee-splitting or setting fees and paying a registered practitioner token amounts; failing to provide clients with notice or contact information of the registered practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order cites In re Piccone, In re Colitz, In re Shia, In re Kroll, and other cases demonstrating that these factual patterns have supported findings of unauthorized practice, deceit, and prejudice to the administration of justice. These examples function as applied guidance in adjudicating similar facts.
